keyVerseText: Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and, lo, it shall not be bound up to be healed , to put a roller to bind it, to make it strong to hold the sword.
rootMeaning: The root of חִתּוּל (chittûwl) is חָתַל (châthal), which conveys the action of swathing or wrapping tightly. This root suggests an image of something being entwined or enveloped securely, emphasizing the literal sense of binding or wrapping around. Beyond the English gloss 'bandage' or 'roller,' the root meaning highlights the function of enclosing or protecting by a close, deliberate wrapping, which conveys care and containment.
usageInScripture: The word חִתּוּל appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Ezekiel 30:21, where it is translated as 'a roller.' This consistent translation as a bandage or roller reveals a focused semantic range centered on the idea of something used to bind or support a broken limb. The singular occurrence emphasizes its specialized meaning related to medical or protective binding, rather than a broader or metaphorical usage.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding חִתּוּל as a bandage or roller enriches our grasp of biblical imagery related to healing and restoration. In Scripture, physical binding often symbolizes God's care and the hope of recovery, even amid judgment or brokenness. The root meaning of swathing reflects God's protective and redemptive work, enfolding His people in grace and strength. This word reminds believers that God’s healing is both tender and firm, providing support that enables endurance and ultimate restoration through Christ.
keyVerseReflection: Ezekiel 30:21 states, 'Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and, lo, it shall not be bound up to be healed, to put a roller to bind it, to make it strong to hold the sword.' Here, חִתּוּל as 'roller' vividly conveys the idea of binding a broken arm to enable strength and function. The word underscores the severity of God's judgment on Pharaoh, indicating that no healing bandage or support will restore his power. This highlights both the finality of divine judgment and the absence of restoration for those opposing God's purposes.
